extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers, and policymakers interested in misinformation and disinformation in Canada
extracted.subtask_description: A chronological, crowd-editable Wikipedia timeline documenting notable incidents, campaigns, responses, and research about misinformation, disinformation, and malinformation in Canada. The page is intended as a dynamic reference for events and sources related to information disorder in the Canadian context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynamic list / completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: This is a dynamic list and may never be able to satisfy particular standards for completeness. You can help by editing the page to add missing items, with references to reliable sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explicitly acknowledges incompleteness and invites community additions; contributions should include references to reliable sources. Entries may be added over time and the timeline will evolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion scope — exclusion of COVID-19 pandemic misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: This timeline largely excludes COVID-19 misinformation in Canada and conspiracy theories related to the COVID-19 pandemic in Canada.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items specifically about COVID-19 misinformation and pandemic-related conspiracy theories are intentionally omitted from this timeline (they are covered elsewhere); when adding events, ensure they fall within the timeline's stated topical scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinformation — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Disinformation is "false information that is purposely spread to deceive people".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes intent to deceive as the distinguishing feature; uses cited definitions (footnoted). Use this definition when classifying an event as disinformation rather than mere error or rumor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misinformation — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Misinformation is information that is false or misleading, that contradicts consensus by experts in the field or by the "best available evidence".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focuses on content being false/misleading relative to expert consensus or best available evidence; intent is not required for classification as misinformation. Use authoritative expert consensus and evidence when assessing whether a claim qualifies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Malinformation — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Malinformation is content grounded in truth but presented in a misleading or exaggerated way, which can lead to misconceptions and harm. It manipulates factual elements to mislead audiences through distortion or selective emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish malinformation from truthful reporting by checking for contextual distortion, selective emphasis, or presentation intended to mislead; cite examples or analyses when labelling an item as malinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source requirement for timeline entries
rubrics_metrics.description: You can help by editing the page to add missing items, with references to reliable sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entries should be supported by reliable, verifiable sources (news reports, official reports, academic studies). Unsourced or poorly sourced claims are inappropriate for inclusion; prefer primary reporting or reputable analyses when documenting events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope for identifying state-sponsored campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: The timeline identifies and names state-sponsored or foreign government information operations (e.g., "Spamouflage"/"Dragonbridge" described as a Chinese government online disinformation program).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When labelling operations as state-sponsored, rely on reputable cybersecurity reports, government statements, or investigative journalism (e.g., Mandiant, Global Affairs Canada, G7 RRM reports). Avoid asserting state sponsorship without credible attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizing and documenting countermeasures and institutional responses
rubrics_metrics.description: The timeline records institutional responses and countermeasures (examples: G7 Rapid Response Mechanism focusing on foreign-sponsored disinformation; Digital Citizen Initiative funding projects to support democracy and social inclusion; calls by government for platforms to implement policies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document government programs, intergovernmental mechanisms, platform policy changes, and research initiatives with citations. When including such items, note their stated purpose and scope and cite the official sources or reports describing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of expert reports and surveys to assess information environment
rubrics_metrics.description: The timeline cites expert reports and surveys (e.g., McGill's Media Ecosystem Observatory, CCCS cost estimates, Council of Canadian Academies report, Statistics Canada survey) to describe changes in Canada's information ecosystem and public perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use findings from peer-reviewed studies, institutional reports, and national surveys to contextualize events; when adding interpretive claims (e.g., 'fragmenting information landscape', 'erosion of trust'), cite the relevant report and avoid overstating results beyond what the source supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing tools/techniques of information manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The timeline documents specific tactics and technologies used in misinformation/disinformation (e.g., social bots posting at non-human rates, deepfakes, doctored videos, coordinated hashtag campaigns, astroturfing, spamouflage accounts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterize tactics using terminology supported by sources; when attributing techniques to actors or campaigns, reference digital forensic analyses, cybersecurity firm reports, or investigative journalism that demonstrate the technique and coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual reporting guidance — avoid conflating awareness with impact
rubrics_metrics.description: The timeline notes distinctions such as: a phenomenon may be present (e.g., attempts to 'disrupt, misinform and divide') yet be 'uncoordinated', limited in number, and have little if any impact (example: 2015 Canadian federal election comment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When documenting events, include assessments of scale and impact from credible analyses rather than assuming presence implies major effect; cite expertise or studies that evaluate impact.
